newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan leaders banter on phone.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan leaders banter on phone.

text.p: Chuckling and exchanging pleasantries, the prime ministers of India and Pakistan on Thursday spoke for the first time on a telephone "hotline" set up to help dispel mistrust between the two longtime foes.
The five-minute chat sounded more like banter between long lost relatives than a conversation between the leaders of two counties that have fought three wars in half a century.
A relaxed Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral laughed, recited an Urdu couplet and asked after the health of his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif.
"How are you feeling?" Gujral asked Sharif in Urdu during the chat, filmed by Reuters Television.
"I got a letter from your father," Gujral said, leaning back in a chair behind his desk. "Please thank him."
The symbolic chat came before a fresh round of peace talks set to start later on Thursday in Islamabad between the two nations' highest ranking career diplomats.
Gujral and Sharif had agreed to set up the direct phone link between their two offices when they met for the first time in the Maldives last month on the margins of a regional summit.
Gujral, who had recited an Urdu couplet during the Maldives meeting, could not resist going back to poetry.
"What we never thought possible, we are thinking today (Jo kabhi socha na tha, ab wo socha to hai)," Gujral said, adding: "At least we both insisted on thinking."
The conversation was the latest signal by the two leaders that they want the talks that resumed in March after a bitter, three-year hiatus to succeed.
"This signals efforts to improve bilateral relations," the Indian government's spokesman told reporters.

Aides had commented in the Maldives on the affinity between the two leaders, who both come from the Punjab region. Gujral is the first Indian prime minister who was born in a region of the subcontinent which after partition in 1947 formed part of Pakistan.

Pakistani Foreign Secretary Shamshad Ahmed and his Indian counterpart, Salman Haider, were set to begin five days of talks later on Thursday. The two diplomats met in New Delhi in March to restart bilateral talks which had become bogged down in 1994 in disagreement over Kashmir.
Both India and Pakistan stake a claim to the divided Himalayan region, and two of the three wars they have fought since 1947 have been caused by their dispute over Kashmir.
"It's a very good thing that we have established this," the Indian leader, who spoke a mixture of Urdu and English, told Sharif.
"We can often talk to each other on phone. We'll feel better."
